```ts
import { Screen, Canvas, rgb, COLOR_DEFAULT, enterAltScreen, hideCursor } from "nish/term";

const screen = new Screen(80, 24, false);
write(enterAltScreen() + hideCursor());
screen.clear(COLOR_DEFAULT);
screen.text(2, 1, "score 0", rgb(255, 255, 0), COLOR_DEFAULT, 0);
write(screen.flush()); // the whole frame the first time, then only what changed
```

</scalar-grid>

<scalar-detail title="No I/O">

Nothing here reads the terminal or writes to it: a `Screen` turns
the cells a program drew into the string that brings the terminal from the
last frame to this one, and a `KeyDecoder` turns the bytes a program read
into key events. The program writes the string with `write` and reads the
bytes however it reads its input; the size of the terminal, raw mode and the
clock are the caller's, passed in as numbers. So this module reaches no
capability, a test can compare its output byte for byte, and it runs the
same under Node.

</scalar-detail>

<scalar-detail title="A `Screen`">

**A `Screen`** holds `width × height` cells, each a code point, a foreground,
a background and two attributes (bold, inverse), twice over: the frame being
drawn and the frame the terminal was last sent. `flush` walks both and emits
only the cells that differ — a cursor move where it is not already in place,
a style change only where the style differs from the cell before it, and the
glyph's UTF-8 bytes — then makes the drawn frame the sent one. Every glyph is
taken to be one column wide; a wide character (most CJK, most emoji) would
push the rest of its row along, and is the caller's to avoid.

</scalar-detail>

<scalar-detail title="A `Canvas`">

**A `Canvas`** draws pixels on a `Screen`: each cell shows two, one above the
other, with the upper half block "▀" in the top pixel's colour on a background
of the bottom pixel's (and the lower half block "▄" when only the bottom
pixel is set). A terminal cell is about twice as tall as it is wide, so the
pixels come out roughly square.

</scalar-detail>

<scalar-detail title="Colour">

**Colour** is 24-bit RGB, an `i32` `0xRRGGBB` made by `rgb`, or
`COLOR_DEFAULT` for the terminal's own colour. A `Screen` made with
`palette256` set sends each colour as the nearest of the 256-colour palette
instead, for a terminal without true colour; deciding which a terminal has
(`COLORTERM` is the usual sign) is the caller's.

</scalar-detail>

<scalar-detail title="Events">

`KeyDecoder.feed` and `poll` answer `KeyEvent`s, as they always
have. `KeyDecoder.feedEvents(bytes, count, nowMs)` and `pollEvents(nowMs)`
read the same bytes as one stream of `TermEvent`s, whose `type` is an
`EVENT_` constant:

- `EVENT_KEY`, a key with its `KEY_` kind and `code`, its `MOD_` bits
  (`MOD_SHIFT`, `MOD_ALT`, `MOD_CTRL`, `MOD_SUPER`, `MOD_HYPER`, `MOD_META`)
  and its `ACTION_` (`ACTION_PRESS`, `ACTION_REPEAT`, `ACTION_RELEASE`):
  legacy keys, xterm's modified keys and modifyOtherKeys
  (`ESC [ 27 ; m ; c ~`), and the kitty keyboard protocol's
  `ESC [ code ; mods:event ; text u` (sw.kovidgoyal.net/kitty/keyboard-protocol);
- `EVENT_MOUSE`, an SGR report `ESC [ < b ; x ; y M|m` (xterm ctlseqs, mode
  1006, or 1016 in pixels with `pixelMouse` set) with its `MOUSE_` button,
  `ACTION_PRESS`, `ACTION_RELEASE` or `ACTION_MOVE`, and cell `x`, `y`;
- `EVENT_PASTE`, everything between `ESC [ 200 ~` and `ESC [ 201 ~` (xterm
  ctlseqs, "Bracketed Paste Mode") as one `text`, never as keys;
- `EVENT_FOCUS`, `ESC [ I` or `ESC [ O` (mode 1004), `gained` or not;
- `EVENT_REPLY`, every answer a terminal sends to a query — DA, DSR, CPR,
  DECRPM, the kitty flags, XTVERSION and DECRQSS (DCS), OSC, APC — with its
  `introducer`, `prefix`, `params`, `intermediate`, final byte `reply` and
  `text`. A reply never reaches the program as a key. `ESC [ row ; col R` is
  both a cursor position report and F3 with modifiers, so a caller that asks
  for one (`ESC [ 6 n`) adds 1 to `cprOutstanding`, and while it is above 0
  the next `R` is the reply, taking 1 off. Nothing expires it: a caller
  that gives up waiting for a report sets it back to 0;
- `EVENT_RESIZE` and `EVENT_QUIT`, which the caller and `KeyState` make.

</scalar-detail>

An unfinished sequence is held for `escapeTimeoutMs` after the last byte arrived,
then given up by `pollEvents` as `feed` would; a control string cut off by
the timeout is dropped whole. A paste is never timed out. A CSI reply cut
off by the timeout (a terminal that stalls inside `ESC [ ? 6 2 c`) cannot
be told from keys, so its bytes come out as the keys they spell.

<scalar-detail title="A `KeyState`">

**A `KeyState`** turns those events into which keys are down. `apply(events,
nowMs)` answers the events to act on and `tick(nowMs)` the releases due
meanwhile; `isDown(key, code)` asks. A terminal without the kitty protocol
sends no releases, so while `releasesAreSynthetic` is set (until the first
real release) a key counts as let go when its repeats stop: `firstRepeatMs`
(700 ms) after a press that has not repeated and `releaseGapMs` (100 ms)
after its last repeat. Silence is measured in stream time when the caller has
one: term-io sends an in-order query after each frame and calls `delivered`
with the send time of each one answered, since by then everything the
terminal generated before it has arrived. Measured that way a stall, a burst
or jittery reads delay the watermark as much as the keys, so a held key never
flickers and a tap comes up 700 ms plus one round trip after its press. With
no watermark yet, silence is wall-clock time between `apply`s, which a link
that reads in bursts more than `releaseGapMs` apart can mistake for a key let
go. While acks stop, nothing is released: there is no wall-clock backstop,
and a caller that stops getting answers clears `watermarked` to fall back to
the wall clock. term-io does so once 1000 ms pass with no query answered,
frames sent or not, which no working link reaches while it draws.
Within one read the caller `apply`s its events before calling `delivered` for
the answer it carries: a `tick` between the two would judge keys against a
watermark that already covers repeats not yet applied, and report a release
and then a press. A non-finite time is ignored. Under X11 and Windows only
the last key pressed auto-repeats, so holding W and then pressing D lets W go
`releaseGapMs` after its last repeat. A real release of a key not down is
dropped, so one arriving after its key was made up as released is not
reported twice. Under kitty a real release that is lost leaves its key down
until focus is lost, and for good without focus reporting. A key the batch
`apply` takes names stays down. A made-up release carries the code and
modifiers the key last came with. Losing focus lets every key go, and Ctrl-C
becomes `EVENT_QUIT` while `quitOnCtrlC` is set. Under the kitty protocol a
non-Latin layout sends Ctrl-C as its own letter (`ESC [ 1089 ; 5 u` for
Russian С), which is not read as a quit: the base-layout key that flag 4
(report alternate keys) adds is not read yet.

</scalar-detail>

<scalar-detail title="The same bytes under Node">

Natively a string is UTF-8 bytes, and `flush`
builds its answer as bytes and makes one string of them. Under Node a string
is UTF-16 units and `write` encodes it as UTF-8, so there `flush` decodes the
same bytes into code units first: the terminal receives the same bytes either
way, which `tests/run.js` checks ("nish/term prints the same bytes under
runtime/nish.mjs"). `text` reads a string's code points as UTF-8 natively and
as UTF-16 under Node, so a string literal draws the same cells both ways.
A `TermEvent`'s `text` is made from bytes the terminal sent: natively it
holds them as they came, and under Node they are decoded as UTF-8 without
checking, so malformed UTF-8 in a paste or reply can differ between the two.
Integer division is spelled `(a / b) | 0`, which truncates in both.

</scalar-detail>

## Classes

### Canvas

Pixels on a `Screen`, two to a cell: `width` is the screen's columns and
`height` twice its rows. Each pixel is a colour or `COLOR_DEFAULT`, which is
the terminal's background showing through. Drawing a pixel redraws its cell
at once, so text drawn after it lands on top, and pixels drawn after text
replace it.

```ts
class Canvas
```

| Member | |
| --- | --- |
| `new Canvas(screen: Screen)` | A canvas of `screen`'s size, every pixel `COLOR_DEFAULT`. Make a new one after the screen is resized. |
| `height: i32` | Pixels down: twice the screen's height. |
| `pixels: i32[]` | One colour per pixel, row by row. |
| `screen: Screen` | The screen the pixels are drawn on. |
| `width: i32` | Pixels across: the screen's width. |
| `clear(colour: i32): void` | Set every pixel to one colour. |
| `fillRect(x: i32, y: i32, w: i32, h: i32, colour: i32): void` | Fill a rectangle, clipped to the canvas. |
| `line(x0: i32, y0: i32, x1: i32, y1: i32, colour: i32): void` | Draw a line, both ends included (Bresenham's). Any `i32` ends will do: the walk stops once it leaves the canvas for good, though one that starts far outside steps all the way in. |
| `pixel(x: i32, y: i32): i32` | What colour a pixel is. |
| `setPixel(x: i32, y: i32, colour: i32): void` | Set one pixel; a pixel off the canvas is not drawn. |
| `text(col: i32, row: i32, s: string, fg: i32): i32` | Draw a string in screen cells over the pixels, each character on the colour of the pixels behind it (the top one, or the bottom one where the top is unset). |

### FixedStep

A fixed-step clock: it turns the time between frames into a whole number of
steps of `1000 / stepsPerSecond` milliseconds, so a game's logic runs at the
same rate whatever the display does. `advance(nowMs)` answers how many steps
to run since the last call and keeps the remainder for the next; `alpha()`
is that remainder as a fraction of a step, to draw between the last two
states. At most `maxSteps` run per call: a clock further behind drops the
backlog rather than spiral, keeping its phase. With `maxSteps` 1 the same
clock paces drawing, answering 1 when a frame is due. The clock is the
caller's, as `KeyDecoder`'s is.

```ts
class FixedStep
```

| Member | |
| --- | --- |
| `new FixedStep(stepsPerSecond: i32, maxSteps: i32)` | A clock for a simulation that steps at a fixed rate whatever the frame rate. |
| `maxSteps: i32` | The most steps one `advance` answers. |
| `stepMs: f64` | The length of one step, in milliseconds. |
| `advance(nowMs: f64): i32` | The steps to run for the time between the last call and now. The first call only starts the clock and answers 0, as does a time earlier than the last one. |
| `alpha(): f64` | How far into the next step the clock is, for drawing between two steps. |

### KeyDecoder

Bytes from a terminal in raw mode, turned into key events. A read can end
in the middle of an escape sequence or a UTF-8 character; the decoder keeps
the start and finishes it with the next `feed`. An ESC on its own is both the
escape key and the start of every arrow, so it is held until either more
bytes complete a sequence or `escapeTimeoutMs` passes with none, and then it
is `KEY_ESCAPE`. Whatever is held past the timeout is given up the same way:
the ESC as `KEY_ESCAPE`, the bytes after it as keys of their own, and an
unfinished UTF-8 character as U+FFFD. The clock is the caller's: each call
takes the time now in milliseconds, from any origin, so long as it does not
go backwards.

`feedEvents` and `pollEvents` decode the same bytes into `TermEvent`s
instead: keys with their modifiers and press, repeat or release, the mouse,
pastes, focus and the terminal's replies, none of which reaches the program
as a key. A decoder is fed one way or the other, not both. The module
header lists every sequence they read.

```ts
class KeyDecoder
```

| Member | |
| --- | --- |
| `new KeyDecoder(escapeTimeoutMs: f64)` | A decoder with nothing held. |
| `cellHeightPx: i32` | A cell's height in pixels, to turn a 1016 report into a row; 0 while unknown. |
| `cellWidthPx: i32` | A cell's width in pixels, to turn a 1016 report into a column; 0 while unknown. |
| `cprOutstanding: i32` | How many cursor position reports (`ESC [ 6 n`) are awaited. `ESC [ r ; c R` is both the report and F3 with modifiers; while this is above 0 it is the report, and takes one off. Whoever writes the request adds one. |
| `escapeTimeoutMs: f64` | How long a held ESC waits for the rest of a sequence, in milliseconds. |
| `pixelMouse: boolean` | Whether SGR mouse reports are in pixels (mode 1016), so `px` and `py` are set and `x`, `y` derived. |
| `feed(bytes: u8[], count: i32, nowMs: f64): KeyEvent[]` | Decode what was read, after whatever was held: held bytes older than the timeout are given up first, as keys of their own, and the rest continue into these. |
| `feedEvents(bytes: u8[], count: i32, nowMs: f64): TermEvent[]` | Decode what was read into events of every kind, after whatever was held, as `feed` takes them. The timeout counts from the last byte that arrived, so a reply split across reads is not given up halfway. |
| `poll(nowMs: f64): KeyEvent[]` | Give up held bytes once the timeout has passed since they arrived. |
| `pollEvents(nowMs: f64): TermEvent[]` | Give up held bytes once the timeout has passed: an ESC as `KEY_ESCAPE`, an unterminated DCS, APC or OSC as nothing. A paste waits for its end however long it takes. |
| `waiting(): boolean` | Whether bytes are held, so the caller should `poll` once the timeout has passed. |

### KeyEvent

```ts
class KeyEvent
```

| Member | |
| --- | --- |
| `new KeyEvent(kind: i32, code: i32)` | A key event. |
| `code: i32` | The character's code point, the control byte, or the escape sequence's final byte. |

### KeyState

Which keys are down, from the events a `KeyDecoder` made — what a game asks
each frame. Under the kitty protocol with event types (flag 2) a terminal
sends real releases. Without it a terminal sends nothing when a key comes
up, only the press again as it auto-repeats, so a key is let go once its
repeats stop: `releaseGapMs` after its last repeat, and `firstRepeatMs` after
a press that has not repeated. The system waits before its first repeat —
660 ms under X11 by default, 500 under Windows, shorter under macOS — and
repeats every 30–40 ms; a longer delay needs `firstRepeatMs` raised, and a
slower rate `releaseGapMs`. Input arrives late and in bursts (over SSH, reads
150–250 ms apart are usual), so when the reads alone are known the silence
is not: a caller that sends in-order queries calls `delivered(sentAtMs)` as
each is answered, and silence is then measured against that watermark rather
than the clock. A key last seen in a read at `A` is let go once the watermark
reaches `A + gap`: had it still been down, the terminal would have generated
a repeat before then, and it would have arrived ahead of the answer. Until
the first `delivered`, and after the caller clears `watermarked`, the gap is
measured against `nowMs`. Pure, with the caller's clock, as `KeyDecoder` is.

```ts
class KeyState
```

| Member | |
| --- | --- |
| `new KeyState()` | No key down, releases synthesized, Ctrl-C a quit. |
| `firstRepeatMs: f64` | How long the system waits before a held key's first repeat, at most, in milliseconds (700 by default, above X11's 660). |
| `quitOnCtrlC: boolean` | Whether Ctrl-C (byte 3, or kitty `ESC [ 99 ; 5 u`) becomes `EVENT_QUIT` (true by default). |
| `releaseGapMs: f64` | How long after its last repeat a key is let go, in milliseconds (100 by default). |
| `releasesAreSynthetic: boolean` | Whether releases are made up from silence; false from the first real release, or when the caller knows kitty flag 2 is on. |
| `watermarked: boolean` | Whether silence is measured against `watermarkMs` rather than the clock; set by `delivered`, which the caller may clear when answers stop. |
| `watermarkMs: f64` | The latest send time of an answered query that `delivered` was given: everything the terminal generated before it has arrived. |
| `apply(events: TermEvent[], nowMs: f64): TermEvent[]` | Take the events of one read and answer what the program should see: first the releases `tick` makes for the keys the events do not mention (a held key's repeats can wait in a read longer than the gap), then each event, with Ctrl-C as `EVENT_QUIT` (its repeats and release dropped) and a press of a key already down marked `ACTION_REPEAT` while releases are synthetic.<br><br>A real release of a key not down is dropped: it was let go already, made up from silence or by losing focus. Losing focus lets every key go, since its release goes elsewhere. |
| `delivered(sentAtMs: f64): void` | Note that everything the terminal generated before a time has arrived: the answer to an in-order query sent then has come back. From now on silence is measured against the latest such time. |
| `deliveredAgoMs(nowMs: f64): f64` | How long ago the latest answered query was sent; the caller clears `watermarked` once this passes its bound. |
| `isDown(key: i32, code: i32): boolean` | Whether a key is down. A letter is the same key in either case, since Shift changes the code a terminal sends. |
| `tick(nowMs: f64): TermEvent[]` | The releases due while releases are synthetic: each key whose gap has passed, let go. |

```ts
class Screen
```

| Member | |
| --- | --- |
| `new Screen(width: i32, height: i32, palette256: boolean)` | A screen of blank cells in the terminal's colours, none of them sent yet, so the first `flush` draws them all. |
| `attrs: i32[]` | The frame's attributes, laid out as `glyphs`: `ATTR_BOLD` and `ATTR_INVERSE`, or'd. |
| `bgs: i32[]` | The frame's backgrounds, laid out as `glyphs`. |
| `fgs: i32[]` | The frame's foregrounds, laid out as `glyphs`: a colour or `COLOR_DEFAULT`. |
| `glyphs: i32[]` | The frame being drawn, one code point per cell, row by row. |
| `height: i32` | Rows. |
| `palette256: boolean` | Whether colours go out as 256-colour palette indices rather than 24-bit RGB. |
| `sync: boolean` | Whether a `flush` that changes anything is wrapped in `beginSync` and `endSync`; off until set. |
| `width: i32` | Columns. |
| `clear(background: i32): void` | Blank every cell of the frame being drawn. |
| `flush(): string` | Turn the frame last sent into the frame drawn, and make the drawn frame the sent one.<br><br>Changed cells are visited row by row. The cursor is moved only when it is not already at the cell — `ESC [ n C` along the row, `ESC [ row ; col H` otherwise — and a gap of up to three unchanged ASCII cells in the current style is rewritten instead, which is shorter than the move. A style is sent only when it differs from the previous cell's, and only the parts that differ, from a reset when an attribute has to be turned off. A flush that leaves the terminal in a style other than the default ends with `ESC [ 0 m`, so what the caller writes next starts plain. With `sync` set, a flush that changes anything is wrapped in `beginSync` and `endSync`, in the same string, so the terminal paints the frame whole. |
| `glyphAt(x: i32, y: i32): i32` | What the frame being drawn holds in a cell. |
| `invalidate(): void` | Forget what the terminal shows, so the next `flush` sends every cell: after a `clearScreen`, say. |
| `resize(width: i32, height: i32): void` | Make the screen a new size, blank and unsent: a terminal that changed size is redrawn in full. Each side is at most 4,096 cells and the screen at most 1,048,576, rows dropped to fit, so no size a terminal reports makes it overflow or run out of memory. |
| `set(x: i32, y: i32, glyph: i32, fg: i32, bg: i32, attrs: i32): void` | Draw one character in a cell; a cell off the screen is not drawn. |
| `text(x: i32, y: i32, s: string, fg: i32, bg: i32, attrs: i32): i32` | Draw a string along a row, one cell per character, clipped at the edges. |

### TermEvent

One thing a terminal sent: a key, the mouse, a paste, a focus change or an
answer to a query, told apart by `type` (an `EVENT_` constant). Each type
fills its own fields and leaves the rest at their defaults: 0, -1 for the
pixel position, "" and no params.

```ts
class TermEvent
```

| Member | |
| --- | --- |
| `new TermEvent(type: i32)` | An event with every field but its type at its default. |
| `action: i32` | An `ACTION_` constant: whether a key or button went down, repeated, came up or (the mouse) moved. |
| `button: i32` | The mouse's `MOUSE_` button. |
| `code: i32` | A key's code: the code point for `KEY_CHAR`, the byte for a control, the kitty key number or the final byte for `KEY_UNKNOWN`. |
| `gained: boolean` | For `EVENT_FOCUS`, whether the terminal gained focus. |
| `intermediate: i32` | A reply's intermediate byte, such as the `$` of DECRPM, or 0. |
| `introducer: i32` | What opened a reply: `[` for a CSI, `P` for a DCS, `_` for an APC, `]` for an OSC, `^` for a PM, `X` for an SOS. |
| `key: i32` | A key's `KEY_` kind. |
| `modifiers: i32` | The `MOD_` bits held with a key or a mouse event. |
| `params: i32[]` | A reply's numeric parameters, an omitted one as 0; for an OSC, its number; for `KEY_UNKNOWN`, the sequence's. |
| `prefix: i32` | A reply's private marker, `?`, `>`, `=` or `<`, or 0. |
| `px: i32` | The mouse's pixel column, from 0, under mode 1016; -1 otherwise. |
| `py: i32` | The mouse's pixel row, from 0, under mode 1016; -1 otherwise. |
| `reply: i32` | A reply's final byte (`c`, `R`, `y`, …); for an APC, its first payload byte (`G` for kitty graphics); for an OSC, 0. |
| `text: string` | A paste's text, a kitty key's associated text, or the payload of a reply after its header. |
| `type: i32` | One of the `EVENT_` constants. |
| `x: i32` | The mouse's column, from 0; -1 under mode 1016 while the cell size is unknown. |
| `y: i32` | The mouse's row, from 0; -1 under mode 1016 while the cell size is unknown. |

## Constants

<scalar-card title="4" icon="phosphor/regular/hash">

`ACTION_MOVE: i32`

The mouse moved, with `button` held or `MOUSE_NONE`.

</scalar-card>

<scalar-card title="1" icon="phosphor/regular/hash">

`ACTION_PRESS: i32`

A key or button went down.

</scalar-card>

<scalar-card title="3" icon="phosphor/regular/hash">

`ACTION_RELEASE: i32`

A key or button came up.

</scalar-card>

<scalar-card title="2" icon="phosphor/regular/hash">

`ACTION_REPEAT: i32`

A held key repeated.

</scalar-card>

<scalar-card title="1" icon="phosphor/regular/hash">

`ATTR_BOLD: i32`

The bold attribute bit: SGR 1.

</scalar-card>

<scalar-card title="2" icon="phosphor/regular/hash">

`ATTR_INVERSE: i32`

The inverse-video attribute bit, foreground and background swapped: SGR 7.

</scalar-card>

<scalar-card title="0" icon="phosphor/regular/hash">

`ATTR_NONE: i32`

No attributes: plain text.

</scalar-card>

<scalar-card title="-1" icon="phosphor/regular/hash">

`COLOR_DEFAULT: i32`

The terminal's own colour, foreground or background: SGR 39 and 49.

</scalar-card>

<scalar-card title="4" icon="phosphor/regular/hash">

`EVENT_FOCUS: i32`

A `TermEvent` that is a focus change, `ESC [ I` or `ESC [ O`: `gained` says which.

</scalar-card>

<scalar-card title="1" icon="phosphor/regular/hash">

`EVENT_KEY: i32`

A `TermEvent` that is a key: `key`, `code`, `modifiers` and `action`.

</scalar-card>

<scalar-card title="2" icon="phosphor/regular/hash">

`EVENT_MOUSE: i32`

A `TermEvent` that is the mouse: `button`, `action`, `modifiers`, the cell `x`, `y` and, under mode 1016, the pixel `px`, `py`.

</scalar-card>

<scalar-card title="3" icon="phosphor/regular/hash">

`EVENT_PASTE: i32`

A `TermEvent` that is a bracketed paste: `text` is everything between `ESC [ 200 ~` and `ESC [ 201 ~`.

</scalar-card>

<scalar-card title="7" icon="phosphor/regular/hash">

`EVENT_QUIT: i32`

A `TermEvent` that asks the program to quit: what `KeyState` makes of Ctrl-C.

</scalar-card>

<scalar-card title="6" icon="phosphor/regular/hash">

`EVENT_REPLY: i32`

A `TermEvent` that is the terminal answering a query: `introducer`, `prefix`, `params`, `intermediate`, `reply` and `text`. Never a key.

</scalar-card>

<scalar-card title="5" icon="phosphor/regular/hash">

`EVENT_RESIZE: i32`

A `TermEvent` that is a new terminal size. The decoder never makes one: it is for the code that watches the size.

</scalar-card>

<scalar-card title="11" icon="phosphor/regular/hash">

`KEY_BACKSPACE: i32`

Backspace: DEL (127) or BS (8), which is the byte's `code`.

</scalar-card>

<scalar-card title="1" icon="phosphor/regular/hash">

`KEY_CHAR: i32`

A printable character; the event's `code` is its code point.

</scalar-card>

<scalar-card title="12" icon="phosphor/regular/hash">

`KEY_CONTROL: i32`

Any other control byte below 32; the event's `code` is the byte (Ctrl-A is 1).

<scalar-card title="9" icon="phosphor/regular/hash">

Ctrl-C, byte 3, which a terminal in raw mode delivers instead of a signal.
